assessmentSummary.identity: A static staggered two-point start followed by high-intent linear acceleration through a 10-yard target.
currentCardFindings: The description matches 2-Point Acceleration Start and differs only by the synonyms split stance, the 10-yard dose, and cone logistics.
Calling it cone-based risks misclassification as agility even though the cone is only a start or finish marker.
All four inherited media links show unrelated cone, build-up, generic sprint-mechanics, or agility content and must be superseded.
Uniform 50-point values omit absolute load, supervision, failure consequence, impact, and work-capacity specificity.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: stance, projection, first steps, and split performance remain repeatable

athleteInstructions: Start still from the assigned split stance and accelerate through the 10-yard line

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Merge into 2-Point Acceleration Start. Preserve Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration as an alias, 10 yards as dosage, and cones as optional logistics; supersede the four mismatched legacy media links.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration is a cone-based athletic drill focused on explosive first two steps from a staggered stance. One start cone and one finish cone 10 yards away. It belongs in the library because it is easy to set up, easy to coach, and scalable from youth development to advanced field/court athletes.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start position and procedure influence sprint performance and must be specified.

Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration is the same static staggered two-point short-acceleration identity as 2-Point Acceleration Start. Calling the stagger a split stance and adding a 10-yard cone does not create a new exercise.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Sprint-start push-off and early acceleration are connected but distinguishable phases.

Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration belongs to static two-point short acceleration. A cone is a target; walking, falling, hand-supported, resisted, and externally cued starts require controlled variants.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Sprint acceleration requires coordinated hip, knee, and ankle action, including hamstring contribution to horizontal force production.
Represent gluteal, hamstring, quadriceps, hip-flexor, plantar-flexor, foot, pelvic, trunk, and reciprocal arm-action roles.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Effective early acceleration is associated with forward-directed impulse and propulsive force.
Use a repeatable stagger, load the stance, project and push backward, coordinate opposite arm and leg, rise progressively, and sprint through the target without forcing universal step positions.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start position influences sprint timing and body position.

Score technical complexity, absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty directly. Athlete experience is programming context, not an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Power output is highest during the first acceleration steps.

Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration must track effort count, distance, sprint contacts, start-side distribution, surface, posterior-chain and plantar-flexor stress, technical fatigue, speed loss, recovery, and total session sprint volume.
Quality sprint work requires a suitable surface, marked target, spacing, run-out, and recovery.
Require a clear dry level 10-yard lane, a stable staggered start, target, athlete separation, and safe run-out; cones, timing gates, and video are optional logistics or measurement tools.
Acceleration work should specify distance, intensity, repetitions, sets, and recovery.
Use two to six high-quality 10-yard efforts with roughly 60–150 seconds recovery, alternating the intended lead side where appropriate and stopping before material speed or technical loss.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Start setup should support propulsion without forcing an anthropometrically inappropriate stance.
Set the stagger, load the front leg, project forward, push the ground back, coordinate the arms, sprint through the 10-yard target, and decelerate in the run-out.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Training should use appropriate supervision, correct technique, manageable demands, and gradual progression.
Stop for pain, limp, slip, stumble, unsafe spacing, lane obstruction, repeated false step, loss of projection or coordination, marked speed decline, or unsafe run-out.
Acceleration and maximal-velocity sprinting are distinct qualities.
Split-Stance 10-Yard Acceleration belongs after preparation and before fatiguing work; it is output practice, not a generic cone-agility drill or dense conditioning interval.
Acceleration develops across successive steps rather than through an immediate upright posture.
Show the stagger from both sides, lead-side options, first three contacts, 10-yard line, run-through behavior, run-out, and a standing-start regression.
Coaches should distinguish acceleration output from maximal velocity and conditioning.
Provide stance and lane checks, start-side balance, side and rear observation, first-step and split timing when used, speed-loss stops, contact totals, and exact alias and variant guidance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed training should be developmentally appropriate and based on movement competency.
Accessibility options include a taller stagger, standing start, submaximal intent, five-yard target, untimed efforts, visual marks, fewer efforts, extra demonstration, and longer recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start position and procedure change the task and measured performance.

Split stance and two-point stance are the same supported geometry here; distance and cones are dosage or logistics, while moving, falling, three-point, reaction, and resisted starts require controlled variants.
